questions.question: What is the primary definition and purpose of a function in R programming?
options: A function is a permanent storage device for saving files to the hard drive
A function is a reusable block of code designed to perform a specific task when called
A function is an error log that records program crashes
A function is a built-in mathematical formula that can never be modified
questions.hint: Functions allow programmers to write logic once and reuse it many times.
questions.explanation: A function is a self-contained, reusable block of code that takes inputs, performs a defined set of instructions, and produces an output, preventing duplicate code.

questions.question: What happens when you define a function in R using 'my_fun <- function() { print(10) }' without calling it?
options: The number 10 is immediately printed to the console
R stores the function definition in memory, but does not execute the body code until the function is invoked with 'my_fun()'
R deletes the function after 5 seconds
A syntax error is thrown because every function must execute upon declaration
questions.hint: Defining creates the recipe; calling actually cooks the meal.
questions.explanation: Defining a function merely binds the code instructions to a variable name in memory. The body code executes only when the function is explicitly called with parentheses.

questions.question: In the function definition 'greet <- function(name) { ... }' and the call 'greet("Aman")', what are 'name' and '"Aman"' called respectively?
options: 'name' is an argument; '"Aman"' is a parameter
'name' is a parameter; '"Aman"' is an argument
Both are called operators
Both are called return values
questions.hint: Parameters are defined in the signature; arguments are the real data values passed at runtime.
questions.explanation: A parameter is the variable declared in the function definition header ('name'), while an argument is the concrete value supplied during the function call ('"Aman"').

questions.question: How do named arguments differ from positional arguments when calling a function in R?
options: Named arguments can be supplied in any order because R matches them by their parameter names
Named arguments only accept character strings
Positional arguments are always executed in reverse alphabetical order
Named arguments are deprecated in modern R versions
questions.hint: When you specify 'arg_name = value', position no longer matters.
questions.explanation: Positional arguments rely on the exact left-to-right order of definition, whereas named arguments explicitly tag parameters by name (e.g. 'tax = 5, price = 100'), allowing flexible ordering.

questions.question: In the function 'calc <- function(price, discount = 0) { ... }', what happens if the caller executes 'calc(150)'?
options: R halts with an error because 'discount' was omitted
The function executes with price = 150 and uses the default value discount = 0
discount is automatically set to NULL
The function asks the user to type a discount in the console
questions.hint: Default values act as automatic fallbacks when optional arguments are not supplied.
questions.explanation: Because 'discount = 0' provides a default argument, omitting it during the call causes R to smoothly assign 0 to 'discount' without throwing an error.

questions.question: What is the crucial difference between 'print()' and 'return()' inside an R function?
options: There is no difference; both perform the exact same task
'print()' only displays text to the console, while 'return()' passes the computed value back to the calling code for storage or further calculation
'return()' can only send back character strings, while 'print()' handles numbers
'print()' terminates the function immediately, while 'return()' repeats the function
questions.hint: If you want to store a result in a variable like 'res <- my_func()', the function must return the value, not just print it.
questions.explanation: 'print()' is a side-effect function that renders information onto the screen, whereas 'return()' hands the computed object back to the caller so it can be assigned to a variable or used in subsequent operations.

questions.question: In R, what is the implicit return behavior if a function body does not contain an explicit 'return()' statement?
options: The function returns NULL in all cases
The function automatically returns the value of the last evaluated expression in its body
The function triggers a fatal compile error
The function restarts from the first line
questions.hint: In R, the final expression evaluated before exiting is the default output.
questions.explanation: R functions automatically return the value of the final expression evaluated in the body block, even if the keyword 'return()' is not written.

questions.question: Because an R function can only return a single object, how can a user-defined function return multiple related statistical values (e.g. mean, min, and max)?
options: By writing multiple return() statements consecutively
By packaging the values together into a single composite object such as a list or named vector
R functions cannot calculate more than one number
By using the repeat keyword
questions.hint: A list can bundle multiple named items into a single container.
questions.explanation: A function can bundle multiple related metrics into a single data structure, most commonly a list (e.g. 'return(list(mean = m, min = mn, max = mx))'), which the caller can unpack using the '$' operator.

questions.question: If a variable 'x <- 10' is created inside a function, what happens if code outside the function attempts to access 'x'?
options: It prints 10 because all variables in R are global
R throws an error ('object 'x' not found') because 'x' is a local variable restricted to the function's private environment
It prints 0 as a default fallback
It converts 'x' into an environment object
questions.hint: Local variables exist only during the lifetime of the function call.
questions.explanation: Variables declared inside a function have local scope; they are created in the function's private execution environment and discarded upon completion, making them inaccessible from outer scopes.

questions.question: What principle governs how R searches for variable values when a variable is referenced inside a function but not defined locally?
options: Dynamic register allocation
Lexical scoping (R searches enclosing environments outward to the global workspace)
Random keyword resolution
Alphabetical file search
questions.hint: R looks outward from the local scope to the enclosing environment where the function was created.
questions.explanation: Under R's lexical scoping rules, if a variable is not found in the local function environment, R looks outward into the enclosing environment (such as the global workspace) where the function was defined.

questions.question: Why is the superassignment operator '<<-' generally discouraged for beginners writing functions?
options: Because it is not supported in base R
Because it modifies variables in enclosing or global environments, introducing hidden side-effects that make code difficult to debug and test
Because it slows down execution by 100 times
Because it can only store complex numbers
questions.hint: Functions should ideally be self-contained without mutating global program state unexpectedly.
questions.explanation: Superassignment ('<<-') bypasses the local scope to mutate variables in outer environments. This creates side-effects, tightly couples functions to global state, and violates clean modular programming principles.

questions.question: What essential component must every recursive function contain to avoid a stack overflow crash?
options: A while loop
A base condition (stopping condition) that halts further self-calls when a boundary is reached
An external C compiler
At least three parameters
questions.hint: Without a stopping check, the function will call itself infinitely.
questions.explanation: A recursive function calls itself to solve smaller subproblems and must have a base condition (e.g. 'if (n <= 1) return(1)') that terminates the recursion before memory resources are exhausted.

questions.question: What happens if a beginner enters 'my_function' in the R console without typing parentheses 'my_function()'?
options: The function executes with default parameters
R prints the function's underlying source code definition instead of executing it
The computer displays a blue screen error
The function is permanently deleted from memory
questions.hint: Typing an identifier by itself displays the object; parentheses tell R to invoke the function.
questions.explanation: In R, typing a function name without parentheses inspects the function object, printing its source code definition to the console. Appending parentheses '()' instructs R to invoke and execute it.

questions.question: If a function is defined as 'add <- function(a, b) { a + b }', what error occurs if called with 'add(10)'?
options: Error: argument 'b' is missing, with no default
Error: index out of bounds
Error: syntax error at end of line
The function executes and returns 10
questions.hint: Parameter 'b' is required and has no fallback value.
questions.explanation: Because parameter 'b' has no default value and the caller supplied only one argument, R halts with: 'Error in add(10): argument "b" is missing, with no default'.

questions.question: In a Machine Learning data pipeline, why is a reusable Min-Max feature scaling function implemented with a safeguard like 'if (max_v == min_v) return(rep(0, length(x)))'?
options: To invert the matrix eigenvalues
To prevent division by zero when all feature values in a vector are identical (e.g. max - min = 0)
To speed up hard drive caching
To convert numeric data to boolean factors
questions.hint: The formula (x - min) / (max - min) fails if max equals min.
questions.explanation: In Min-Max scaling, the denominator is (max - min). If a feature column contains constant values, max equals min and the denominator becomes 0 (resulting in NaN/Inf). Guard conditions ensure robust production pipelines.
